briefing:
The headline Airfare Price Index (APIx) registered at 103.07 for the daily intelligence cycle ending September 13, 2026, representing a aggregate price increase of 3.07% over baseline median levels across surveyed domestic trunk routes. This upward shift reflects a broad-based firming in domestic passenger airfares, introducing short-term inflationary pressure to the transport and communication component of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Market expansion was predominantly driven by the Delhi – Bengaluru corridor, which recorded a route-level APIx of 106.50 (a 6.50% increase over base), while the heavily weighted Delhi – Bombay and Calcutta – Bombay corridors demonstrated more moderate growth, posting route APIx values of 101.70 (+1.70%) and 101.46 (+1.46%), respectively.

Disaggregating the index by advance booking offsets reveals that the inflationary pressure was strongly concentrated in the near-term T+7 departure window, which carries a substantial 30% weight in the macro index. On the Delhi – Bengaluru route, T+7 target median prices escalated to ₹10,169 against a base median of ₹8,609, resulting in a route-window price relativity of 118.12%, complemented by elevated T+30 demand at a 110.62% relativity (₹9,767 vs base ₹8,829). Similarly, the Calcutta – Bombay sector experienced significant short-term tightening at T+7 with a price relativity of 115.25% (target ₹10,420 vs base ₹9,041), while Delhi – Bombay reached 107.37% (target ₹6,843 vs base ₹6,373). Conversely, longer-dated advance purchase windows provided a cooling effect, most visibly in Calcutta – Bombay at T+45 where price relativity dropped to 86.01% (target ₹11,108.50 vs base ₹12,915) and Delhi – Bengaluru at T+15 (95.64% relativity), underscoring carrier yield strategies that heavily penalize late-stage bookings while incentivizing forward capacity utilization.

Granular target-day scrape data reveals pronounced intra-route fare dispersion across carrier business models and secondary regional hubs. Low-cost carriers and expanding budget operators, particularly Akasa Air and Air India Express, regularly anchored the lower bound of price distributions across offsets, providing promotional deal fares that undercut legacy carrier medians; for instance, Air India Express featured a T+7 fare of ₹5,761 on Delhi – Bombay compared to Air India’s direct flight cluster priced at ₹6,843. Furthermore, the active integration of secondary airport infrastructure—including departures from Ghaziabad/Hindon (HDO) and Jewar (DXN), alongside arrivals into Navi Mumbai (NMI)—introduced notable cost-saving entry points into the raw matrix, with Hindon and Navi Mumbai flights frequently undercutting primary city-center airport pairings by ₹100 to ₹400 across T+1, T+15, and T+30 windows.

Looking ahead, domestic airfare momentum is anticipated to maintain a moderate upward bias in the immediate 7-to-14 day horizon as short-term capacity absorption remains tight, before stabilizing as booking volumes shift toward discount-heavy T+30 and T+45 advance purchase horizons. From a monetary policy and statistical perspective, the 3.07% rise in the APIx signals transient upward friction in service sector inflation, warranting continued observation by the Reserve Bank of India and MoSPI regarding potential pass-through risks into core CPI non-food, non-energy segments. Policymakers should continue utilizing high-frequency airfare pipelines to decouple temporary carrier yield optimization spikes from underlying structural trends in domestic transportation service costs.
